analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction for junk food ads aimed at children and redirects the revenue to school fresh produce programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so companies could no longer deduct the cost of advertising or marketing junk food to children 14 and under — including TV, social media, product placement, in-school ads, toy tie-ins, and celebrity endorsements. It would direct the National Academy of Medicine to develop standards for identifying food of poor nutritional quality, and would send every dollar of new tax revenue into the Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program, which provides free fresh produce to schoolchildren. The bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, whose diets and eating habits form early and who are the targets of roughly $2 billion a year in food marketing according to the FTC report cited in the bill. Parents benefit indirectly as fewer junk food ads reach their kids, and schools benefit because the new tax revenue would fund free fresh fruits and vegetables in the Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program.

how_it_helps.text: It removes a federal tax write-off for advertising and marketing junk food to children 14 and under, covering TV, social media, product placement, packaging, celebrity endorsements, event sponsorships, and even in-school advertising like branded scoreboards and vending machines.

It transfers the extra tax revenue collected from that change, dollar for dollar, into the Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program, which provides free fresh produce to children in participating elementary schools.
It directs the National Academy of Medicine to develop the standards for identifying food of poor nutritional quality, taking the definition out of the hands of the companies being regulated.

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage companies and fast-food chains that market to children would pay more in taxes because marketing to kids would no longer be a deductible business expense. Advertising agencies, media outlets, and marketing firms would lose revenue from child-directed food campaigns.

drawbacks.text: Food companies would pay more tax, and some of that cost could be passed on to consumers through higher prices or reduced promotions that families actually use, like coupons and loyalty discounts.

The bill's key term — 'food of poor nutritional quality' — would be defined by Treasury regulations based on a National Academy of Medicine report, and the line between junk food and ordinary groceries is contested, so the rules could be hard to apply and could draw years of dispute over which products and brands are covered.

Because the deduction denial applies to marketing with audiences that are 25 percent or more children, some advertising for mixed-audience media would be swept in, raising costs for food brands even for ads not aimed at children.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real: tax research cited in the bill's findings ties child-directed junk food marketing to children's food choices and long-term health, and redirecting the recovered revenue into the school Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program gives children a direct benefit. The costs are real but modest: food companies would pay somewhat more in taxes, which could be passed to consumers, and the definition of "food of poor nutritional quality" would be contested and litigated, adding compliance complexity. The bill died without any committee action or cosponsors, so none of this was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in November 2022, and neither committee took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill's only recorded actions were its introduction on November 15, 2022 and its referral the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee.
It attracted zero cosponsors in the House.

No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, killing the bill under the rule that bills must pass both chambers within a single two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and beverage companies keep the full tax deduction for marketing to children, and advertising and media businesses keep the ad revenue, because the bill never advanced. Children's health advocates gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food companies and their ad agencies

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition was recorded; the bill drew no cosponsors from either party before it died in committee.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers and fast-food chains
industries.note: They would lose the federal tax deduction for marketing junk food to children — about $2 billion a year in child-directed food marketing per the FTC report cited in the bill. The practical effect is a higher tax bill on that spending, which is designed to push their products less effectively at kids.

Agencies and media outlets that produce and run child-directed food advertising would lose billable work and ad revenue, since clients would scale back campaigns that no longer qualify as a deductible business expense.

The bill would eliminate the tax deduction for in-school advertising — branded materials, scoreboards, vending machine fronts, label redemption programs — which some schools currently receive as sponsorship revenue, while channeling new federal money into the Fresh Fruit and Vegetable Program for elementary schools.
